utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zatriqi, were you a member -- the owner of Flamingo Tours company?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the owners of this agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was your agency established?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agency was established in December 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You actually dealt in transportation, that was your business?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in transportation. Also in transportation and in tourist tours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998 and 1999, did you have to pay double registration?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be more explicit, please, because I'm not so sure about what you are asking me because normally you have to register your cars or your car.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I will show you a document now, and then we'll see whether you're familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have number D002-6060.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, can you read this document, please?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff of the military police administration of the KLA dated 3rd February, 1999, and it refers to the decision by the Main Staff of 31 December 1998 to determine the fees for registration of vehicles and then, among other things, it says under 1 it's up to 900 Deutschemarks; under 2 it says that the fee has to be paid for one year and that it will correspond to the period of registration. So my question is: In addition to the normal registration, regular registration, did you also have to pay for registration in keeping with this decision of the military police administration?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time for me to see such a document. Reading it I can see that you have to pay for vehicles travelling in those areas controlled by KLA. Peje was not one of them; that's why I didn't have a chance to look at such a document or to pay such a fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see, please, the Defence document D002-6058. Thank you. Could we just zoom in a bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, do you recognise this image, this photo?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, relatively, yes. It's a very small picture. It's not easy for me to distinguish clearly the facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know you can't see any facilities. We couldn't do that yesterday either, but could you please just put an X in the area where your house was on this photo?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to do that because it is indeed very small. It must be here, on this part. I can't be accurate in my location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we could try coming in closer to about half the size of the present picture if that is likely to help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps if we can come a little closer still and then maybe we can pull up the photo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this better, Mr. Zatriqi?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is better than before, but still it's a problem for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might have to leave it then, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll move on, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Zatriqi, that in paragraph 8 of your statement, your June 2001 statement, you said: "I did not see the buses again, since that moment on, until I returned in Pec on the 26th of July, 1999." So this refers to the time when you actually handed over the buses, when they were confiscated. Is this paragraph correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I stated. It was not that I handed over the buses, actually. They were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was about this paragraph 8, the first sentence reads: "From that moment I did not see the buses until I returned to Pec on the 26th of July, 1999."

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same paragraph but in the next sentence you said: "The buses were in the same place but burned down." You men when you arrived there on the 26th of July, 1999. Am I correct that you were not an eye-witness to that event, to the burning of the buses?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As you can see from my statement, I returned very late from my exile. So when I came I was faced with such a situation, but I wasn't there to eye-witness what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 10 you state that there was shooting in -- at Kapesnica, but did you happen to notice whether there was any shooting coming from Kapesnica?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no shooting came from Kapeshnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that there was no fire coming from Kapesnica?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it very well because from the back of my house you can have a very good view of Kapeshnice, you can have an entire view of the place, and when I was moving about the house I could see very clearly that no fire came from Kapeshnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Transcript page 3803, lines 23 through 25, and page 3804, lines 1 to 4, of yesterday's transcript you said: "My house was in such a position that I could see the direction from which these shells were fired and where they were headed. These shells were flying over my house. I moved around the house from the third floor and in the area behind the house so I could see the shelling, I could see where the shells were fired from, and what the targets were. The shells fell on a neighbourhood that is across from our neighbourhood and it's called Kapeshnica." Now, Mr. Zatriqi, in paragraph 10 you say that fire was opened on Kapesnica, but you do not say that you've actually observed this. You said that you were in the cellar of your house, in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but at least in the English version that I have, paragraph 10, page 2, the last sentence says exactly: "They were firing at the neighbourhoods of Kapeshnica. I saw this myself."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you were in the basement. Is it correct that you were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Even yesterday I said that my family, my children, my parents were in the basement, whereas I, myself, moved about the house all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said that that's what you stated yesterday; but in your 2001 June statement, in paragraph 10 - and I've just read it out to you - you said the 26th and the 27th of March I stayed in the basement of my house. Does that mean that this portion of your statement is incorrect, your -- this portion of your 2001 statement?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, doesn't mean that it's not accurate, but I meant that I prepared the basement in order to accommodate my family there, to protect them from the shelling because I considered the basement as a very suitable place to hide. But now and again I visited them. I might have stayed there for a while but then went back to the house and moved about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that is not what you said in your June statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you can imply what I meant by placing my family there. Initially I thought to hide there myself, but then I changed my mind. I decided to go up and see what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but please answer my question. This is something that you said later on when you testified before the Court, but in this statement that I've shown to you that is not what is stated. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you are repeating and repeating. There can be no confusion about the position. The statement in the paragraph says that I stayed in the basement in my house for those two days. The last sentence of that paragraph says "I saw this myself," speaking of the firing. The two are not compatible. The witness in his evidence yesterday and repeated again today says the explanation is simple: "My family were in the basement. I was there with them at times but most of the time I moved around the house and I could see clearly from the upper floors of the house where the shooting was occurring and where the shells were landing." Now, what more can he say about that and what more do you hope to get from him? You can put to us later that this is different and what he's now saying is not what he said originally and we will have to weigh up whether that is something we accept or not. But you've got all the facts from the witness, so you're just pressing on for no purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My question was precisely aimed at the fact that this was omitted and it had no other purpose. My question was just: Is it true that you did not say this, that you were in the basement and that you actually did not say so at the time. Thank you. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 3806, this is yesterday's transcript, you said that the Serbian army shelled using tanks. In your June 2006 statement you never mentioned that you saw any artillery or any weapon from which the shelling actually came?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. In my statement, most of it is focused on the deportation of the population. What you are putting to me now are things which I replied in answer to questions asked of me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 3807 of yesterday's transcript, lines 14 through 18, you say: "We left the house on the 27th of March in the morning because the previous night, the night of the 26th on to 27th, fire was opened on our house. My family, my parents and I, hid in the basement. I moved around the house, moving from one part to another, and when the shelling began we decided to leave." All right, you've already answered the part that refers to moving around the house so let's move on. On page 3808, lines 1 through 6, you said: "As I've already mentioned, moving from one part of the house to another, I could clearly see that early in the morning, around 2.00 or 3.00 a.m., a van, a police van, stopped near my house. They talked to my neighbours. There were also neighbours of mine who were armed, and an hour later they started to shoot. They opened fire in the direction of my house." Now, this portion, Mr. Zatriqi, does not exist in your 2001 June statement.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one change. The minivan didn't belong to the police, but I think it was a privately owned one. But this also is an answer to a question I was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please answer my questions. I've read a portion of the transcript and then I just said that this is something that is not -- cannot be found in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit P672, could we display it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you -- in Albanian it's page 3. Mr. Zatriqi, can you find in that statement of June 1999 that part concerning policemen that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere towards the end of the page it says: "We left because there was shooting all night long. There were bullet impacts on my house."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I haven't translation. [Interpretation] Hello? But I can't hear you again. Okay. Right. I hear you now. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, this was quoted by the end of the statement when you stated the reason for leaving Pec, and this passage was from the time when you were still in the house. You did not mention anywhere that policemen had come, that someone had gotten out of the car and what else happened. That was Sunday morning, paragraph 13, that is, two paragraphs above.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the statement we are looking at, later on when I testified I was asked to explain the reasons why we left the house, who was staying in my house, and that's why then I provided the Court with a detailed answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were giving this statement in 2001, were you in a hurry? Was the interviewer in a hurry?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the gentleman who interviewed me was not in a hurry. I was in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 2001, were are you working for the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be fair to say that in paragraph 13, that is, the third paragraph from the top on that last page, in the last sentence you stated: "I did not see any troops"?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I said that, that I didn't see any military, didn't see any police, but when the shelling started, I know that that the shelling was carried out by the army because at that time only the army had tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, that paragraph 13, I understand it refers to your departure from Pec, nothing else. Of course I don't mean that you had never seen any troops, but also you say, When I was going towards Rozaje I didn't see any troops. That's all I meant in that limited context. I did not intend anything ill. I was just asking about this particular context.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were expelled from Peje, I left through a different neighbourhood. There are many houses in that neighbourhood. It is true that en route I didn't see any army members or police or -- on the way --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I only saw police and armed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just used again the word expelled, and I tried to find that word in the statement of June 2001, and to be quite frank, I have not succeeded.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's different wording. Even if you say "we left," we all know why we left. We know the reasons why we left our house. So it would be the same thing to say "expelled" or "leave," because to me it has the same meaning, as I know the reasons why I left my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the reason war?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the reasons in my statement, the firing, the shelling, of course the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zatriqi. And you left to Montenegro, you left for Rozaje in Montenegro; right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had to leave and left in the direction of Rozaje. We were told to take that direction, and from Rozaje we proceeded towards Ulqin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Rozaje is in Montenegro, and at that time Montenegro was part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right, and this was the reason why I left Montenegro 21 days later. Although we were not threatened there, the fact that it was the same country, we decided to leave. We left in the direction of Bosnia, and from Bosnia we took a plane to Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that you did not see yourself how the mosque in Pec was damaged in 1999?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't see the mosque in Peje being damaged or burnt. And not only the mosque in Peje, but I didn't see any mosque being burnt or damaged myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nor did you eye-witness how the houses were damaged in Pec in your absence in 1999; am I right?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. As I already mentioned, I returned rather late from exile, sometime on the 26th of July, so it was impossible for me to see how these houses were damaged or burnt, but 80 per cent of the houses in Peje were damaged or burnt. Among them, my house too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We appear to have a transcript difficulty at the moment. You may have to wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told that the matter may be resolved, although that's not apparent on our screens, so if you would carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the part that is missing from our transcript will be caught up at a later time and inserted, so carry on, Mr. Djurdjic, from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Pec in July 1999, were there any Serbs in Pec?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned in July, I personally didn't come across any Serb. I'm speaking about July 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zatriqi. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have finished my cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. D'Ascoli, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, I only have a few questions for you and then that will be the end of your testimony. First of all, I would like to clarify one part of your statement, and this is page 3, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe if we can have up on the screen the exhibit number -- yeah. If we can go to page 3 of the English and Albanian -- the Albanian is also page 3, please. I'm sorry, the next page. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Zatriqi, I'm referring to the paragraph which says: "We left because all night long there had been shooting, there had been bullet impacts on our house, we were in fear for our lives." You were asked about this paragraph by my learned colleague. I just want to clarify to which moment in time you refer to in this paragraph. If you can help us with that, please.

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This occurred on the night between the 26th and 27th of March sometime in the early morning hours. There was heavy shooting. Fortunately my family was in the basement. They had taken tranquillisers and they were unable to hear. But myself, as I was moving about in the house, I did hear the shooting, and I could clearly see how they were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Therefore, when you say "bullet impacts on our house," to which house are you referring to ?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house, and these were the reasons why we left in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In the morning of which day, if you remember, please?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well. We left from my house on the 27th and went to Jarina to my aunt's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear now. I also want to clarify once again the reasons why you left Pec because my learned colleague asked you about the reasons why you left your home and also you left Pec. Can you please tell us why you and your family left Pec on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, one of the main reasons amongst other reasons was fear for our lives. That's why we left, we joined other people from Peje, and I can tell you that all of us left Peje because of the fear for our lives and not willingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you feel you had a choice to remain in Peje or in your house if you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I had a choice. I think we made the right decision to leave the house. And it turned out that we made the right decision indeed, as when we returned from exile we saw what had happened in Peje, and we could have gotten worse of it if we remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask you, did you leave for fear of the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't fear the NATO bombing at all. Not only me, but in my opinion no one in Kosova feared NATO bombing. We could have been a target, but we didn't fear -- in fact, when we heard that the NATO bombing started against Serbian military targets, my wife and I opened a champagne and had a drink, although this was against our religion, but we did know that that was a good thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I want to clarify another part of your testimony. My learned colleague asked you about a paragraph of your 2001 statement, and this is - if we can go back to the statement on the screen - this is page 2 of the English and page 2 of the Albanian as well. And do you remember you were asked about the paragraph which says so: "From that moment, I did not see the buses anymore until I returned to Peje on the 26th of July, 1999. The buses were in the same place but burned." Do you remember, sir, you made an addendum in 2002 to this statement, this previous statement of 2001?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you tell us the changes that you -- that you inserted in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second statement, I clearly state that in the convoy of vehicles in the direction of Rozaje, I saw my own bus filled with "passengers." All of these people on the bus were Albanian with the exception of the driver who was a policeman dressed in a blue camouflaged uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Mr. Zatriqi: My learned colleague also asked you about whether you saw how the mosque and the houses in Pec were damaged in 1999. I want to ask you: What did you see when you returned to Peje? What did you see, I mean like in which conditions you saw the houses in Peje?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned in Peje I was shocked. 80 per cent of the houses were damaged. I toured the town. I walked about. I saw many houses and religious facilities destroyed and damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you see also mosques and other religious buildings damaged when you returned in Peje?

utterances.speaker: EDISON ZATRIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw the old mosque in my own neighbourhood, in Sahat Kulla, and then the one in the heart of Peje, in the old bazaar, which was like a business quarters with small old shops. Peje was proud of this quarters. At the end of this small street was a mosque called Carshia mosque, and I think it was under the protection of UNESCO. It was completely burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zatriqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Zatriqi, you'll be pleased to know that concludes the questions of the Chamber for you. We are grateful that you've been able to come to The Hague again to assist. We have now not only the evidence you've given yesterday and today, but your earlier statements and the transcript of the evidence you gave at the previous hearings. We thank you for your assistance, and you are, of course, free now to return to your normal activities. The court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, can you hear me? I will like, before the witness comes, in to raise an issue briefly. I read the Rules yesterday, and I couldn't -- I was no wiser. I received from the Prosecution the testimony 92 bis/live for the next witness, Mazrekaj. I really can't understand what kind of evidence that is. Is it 92 bis or is it live? Are we admitting statements or is new evidence offered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is Mr. Behar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not sure precisely what my learned colleague's question is. I know this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He's asking whether you are giving the evidence of the next witness pursuant to 92 bis, in written statement form, or whether he is to be questioned as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: No, in the -- in keeping with our previous questioning, his evidence will be tendered in 92 bis form; however, I will have some brief questions for him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The brief questions will of course be merely elaboration and clarification and not new evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that should satisfy Mr. Djurdjic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is not here yet, so I can say this. The supplement information has 18 paragraphs, and after what I read, I could not really agree that this is an explanation of the previous statement. That's why I believe they qualified it as 92 bis/live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this came up in past, and perhaps I can shed some light in the matter. The supplemental information sheets that are being provided to Mr. Djurdjic, and certainly in the case of Mr. Mazrekaj, are for the purposes of disclosure, and in keeping with our disclosure obligations. And in this case, of course, it's not an indication that we're intending to lead all or any of that evidence; it's simply so that the Defence has any new information that's coming out from that witness. I don't know if this is giving rise to an impression that we're intending to tender all that evidence. I can indicate that's certainly not my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Mr. Behar, because you might have encountered problems had you been trying. It has occurred with one or two earlier witnesses, and hence the Chamber is sensitive and Mr. Djurdjic is sensitive to what was a tendency to really have both ways. So we are now concentrating on Rule 92 bis and the written statement with some limited clarification and elaboration. We await the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. And of course the next witness is Mehmet Mazrekaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could you please provide us with your full name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: My name is Mehmet Mazrekaj from Drenoc village, Decani municipality, born on the 12th of May, 1944.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you were a school teacher at a secondary school in Decan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, a teacher of a high school called Brothers Frasheri in Decan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that on the 4th of February of 2000 you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that occurred in your village in 1998 and 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review that statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, I understand there are a couple of corrections or clarifications that you'd like to make to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could we have up 65 ter number 02374.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were some minor mistakes which I think I improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. And I'll take you through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see we have the statement up on the screen. If we could have it at page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In about the fifth paragraph there and the second line you state - and I'm quoting - "the police was staying in Xhafer Zukaj's house. At the end of that same paragraph it states: "We were told to go to the basement of that house, and they would let us know that in five minutes." And let me ask you to be clear. Are you saying that you were sent to the basement of this same house that the police were in or does a change need to be made?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Something must be changed because I didn't mean the basement where the policemen were but I meant the basement was in another house where we were staying in that basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. So this was a different house; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this other house was roughly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It was almost across the house where the policemen were staying. Only a street separated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now on the next page, and I think it may actually be two pages ahead of what we're showing on the screen here, it's what I show as page 7, it's the page that begins in English with "an hour later..." That's right. Thank you very much. The first line of this page states: "An hour later after we were held there, all villagers were brought to Xhafer Zukaj's house ..." Is this line correct? Were the villagers brought to Mr. Zukaj's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: No. Only some of us who had gone to ask the policemen -- the police how the people -- the population of the village could go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right. Sir, I understand that you explained earlier in your statement that some of you went to Mr. Zukaj's house, but when you're talking about where the villagers were brought is this referring to the different house that you mentioned to me before? Or were villagers being brought to Mr. Zukaj's house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: No, it was another house. They didn't go to Xhafer Zukaj's house because there the police and the army were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And just so we're clear, this other house, is this the same house that you mentioned to me a couple of minutes ago in the first correction?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. The next line states: "My wife, my parents, and two old people were kept outside." My question is: Where were those people kept outside? Was this a different place? Was this a different house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It was another house about 700 metres away from where we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what house that was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: This house was Adem Vishaj from Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. With those changes having been made, are you satisfied that the information contained in this document is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, to my knowledge and belief it is completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that statement, it's 65 ter number 02374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00675, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying at the trial of Milutinovic et al. on the 2nd and 3rd of November, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, do you remember testifying at the trial of Milutinovic et al. on the 2nd and 3rd of November, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to listen to the transcript of your testimony from that trial?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I had a chance to listen to the transcript -- to read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And does that transcript accurately reflect your evidence and would you testify to the same facts today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: What I testified then, they were all accurate. There were, however, a few minor mistakes in the Serbo-Croatian translation of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Was the content of your answers correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: My answers were correct as far as I know. I tried to express them accurately, but the translation was not very good. It should have been in Albanian not in the Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender 65 ter number 05092, transcript of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00676, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can now provide a brief summary of Mr. Mazrekaj's evidence, and I can indicate that it relates chiefly to paragraphs 72(l) and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj is a Kosovar Albanian male school teacher who was born in the village of Drenoc in the Decani municipality. He describes the events of what he calls the first offensive in the summer of 1998, explaining that Serb forces shelled villages within the Decani municipality from a hill and he describes how thousands of villagers were displaced and forced to flee. Mr. Mazrekaj describes the involvement of police and the use of check-points and explains how he fled with his family before ultimately returning home to Drenoc months later. Mr. Mazrekaj also explains the events of 1999, beginning on the 27th of March. He describes that Serb police came to his village of Drenoc and told the Albanians to leave because of the NATO bombing. Mr. Mazrekaj made efforts to arrange for the civilians to leave and to be able to cross through certain check-points. He eventually helped to lead villagers from Drenoc to Beleg. Mr. Mazrekaj describes the events the next day, when police came to Beleg. He explains that police were operating out of the house of a man named Xhafer Zukaj, that he went to that house to try to arrange for Albanian civilians to peacefully leave the village. He was sent to the basement of a nearby house along with large numbers of other Albanian civilians where they were kept at gunpoint, both inside and outside of the house. Mr. Mazrekaj describes the terrible conditions at that house and the serious violence and looting that was visited on himself and on other civilians. He also explains how the men were separated from the women and that he saw that the village itself was being set on fire. He describes how the next day police directed them to leave on tractors, leading them along and then directing them to go towards Albania. Mr. Mazrekaj escaped eventually making his way back to Isniq where he rejoined his family. Serb forces then began shelling Isniq and they fled to Albania. En route police were stopping people and taking their documents and identification. Mr. Mazrekaj stayed in Albania with his family for three months and returned to Kosovo on the 28th of June, 1999. That ends the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I do have some brief clarification questions for you in the limited time that we have. You begin to describe the events of 1999 at page 4 of your statement in the second last paragraph and you describe that on the 27th of March the villagers gathered in the centre of town. Can you tell us when the police arrived in your town that day and what, if anything, was communicated to you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That day the police arrived at around 8.00 in the morning. Some -- they expelled some villagers and they ordered us to vacate the village as soon as we possibly could because of the NATO air-strikes they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And was there any NATO bombing at that time that you observed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The NATO bombing started on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did you experience that in your village?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That day, we left the village and took the road towards Beleg, in order to go to Isniq village. On the way, we had problems because the main roads were blocked, so we had to pass through side-streets until we reached Beleg village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Right. Just to clarify my last question, sir, I was just asking if you experienced bombing yourself. Was your town bombed by NATO that you experienced?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: For the time we were there, it was not bombed. We heard the roar of bombing in the direction of Gjakove and some other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained in your statement that you went twice to a check-point in Carrabreg to speak to police there to arrange to get people out of the village. Can you just clarify for us, who was manning that check-point and who was it that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It is true that I went there two times. I was together with some other villagers. We failed to find an agreement with the police at the check-point in Carrabreg. The leader of that check-point was Zoran Djurisic, a policeman of road traffic police at Decan municipality. The second time, I went together with the local police who were chosen by the police chief to defend our village in order for us to agree with them that they allow the population to pass through this check-point. After we agreed, I returned to the village, but we couldn't go there because during that period the police constantly kept separating the women from men. So we were afraid to go there through the -- that check-point. That's why we found -- we chose another route, to go to Beleg village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And do you explain in your statement that you left Drenoc with the villagers - I know you've just explained that you avoided the police check-points and went to Beleg - you describe in page 5 in the final paragraph of your statement on that page that on the 28th of March, around 1.30 p.m. or 2.00 p.m. the police came to the village. Can you explain to us how many police came at this time, just a rough estimate ? Was it a large number or a small number?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: They came by the police car -- three, there were three of them. One of them was from Peje, I don't recall his name; another one was police driver; and the other was a Roma, police -- he was called Ahmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now at page 6 of your statement in the fifth paragraph, you describe going to talk to the police who were staying at Xhafer Zukaj's house. Can you tell us, were these the same police that you described arriving just now?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: No, they were not the same. They were different. They were different, those ones that were at Xhafer Zukaj's.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So these police who were staying in Xhafer Zukaj's house, can you tell us how and when those police arrived?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: They came at night on the 28th of March, in the evening, and entered the village of Beleg. It was a large group, but there were also soldiers. They were those of Arkan and Seselj who were settled in Felkisa [phoen] and Decan where it was children's kindergarten -- resort.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And the people that you've described as being the forces of Arkan and Seselj, can you explain to us what they looked like, what they were -- how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: They had camouflage clothes. They were painted -- their faces were painted. They had their own vehicles. They had police, army, tanks, vehicles. Beleg was full of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, when you're describing the vehicles, was it only these forces you just described, these paramilitary forces, that had vehicles, or did the police have vehicles as well ? Could you tell?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: There were police vehicles, military vehicles. You could see only the barrels directed towards us; after they took us out of the basement we could see that. So these vehicles had the colours of the army and the police; namely, they were blue and green.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described in your statement going to the police and asking them for permission to leave the village, and you describe how they sent you instead into a basement in a nearby house. Can you describe for this Court what the conditions were like for you and for other people in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That morning, some villagers came from Beleg, from my village, to ask us to go to the police in order to ask their permission for us to go from Beleg to Isniq village. When we went there, the police told us, Come here. We talked with them. They said, After five minutes you have to go to this house. When we went to that house, in the basement, we found some families, women, children, old people. It was a horrible situation because the basement and the house were not finished. They were in the course of construction. From there you could see what was going on outside. We could see the barrels of the guns. Children and women started to cry. In the meantime, other families were being brought in. There I recognised a policeman. He was from Gjakova. I addressed him, and he said to me -- he said, I am not the one that you think I am, but I knew him very well. I only didn't remember his name. So the basement was constantly being filled in with people, with new people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, sir. Can you explain to us, was it crowded and how many people were in that basement with you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: When I initially went there, there were about 20 persons, but the number kept increasing until there was no more room for people to stay in there. So people were staying around the basement, outside, but surrounded by police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, at page 7 of your statement, you described being beaten quite badly by Zoran Djurisic, and you use the -- I'll just quote from your statement. You say: "Zoran would hit me once and other paramilitaries would hit me back." I wanted to clarify with you, was Zoran a police or did he look like part of a paramilitary? Can you explain what forces Zoran was part of?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I know Zoran very well. In 1978 he was a student in the high school where I was teaching, then he went to another school, to the police school in Vushtrri. After finishing that school, he started working in the police station in Decan as a policeman -- as a road police, traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So were there other people there who you would describe as paramilitary who were beating you at that time, as you described?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Most of them were policemen. In the front ranks there was Zoran Djurisic who took away a child I was holding and started to kick me -- to beat me, to hit me with blows and with the rifle-butt. So -- until I fainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this may be a good time for the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Behar. We must now have the first break which will be for half an hour, and we resume at 11.00. You'll understand we have an adjournment now. The court officer will take you to a waiting-room and we continue at 11.00. Thank you. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if we could pick up again where we left off earlier. You described at page 7 of your statement that the local Albanian policemen were also held together with you and that they were disarmed and beaten as well. My question for you is: Can you tell us who those Albanian policemen that you described were?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes. The local Albanian policemen were from my village. They were two brothers, Shaban and Ali Kadrijaj. They were from Drenoc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you describe for us, sir, who was beating them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The police that were there, that had surrounded us. They set them aside, took their badges, and also their weapons that once they issued to them in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your statement a person named Male Vishaj and you described him as "a Serb collaborator." Can you explain to us, to the Court, what you meant by that term, "Serb collaborator"?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Male was from Beleg village. He was an activist in the past, and he was friends with the chief of the police in Decan. He promised to us that nothing was going to happen to us in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So when you say "collaborator," was it just that he was someone who had good relations with the Serbs; is that fair? Or how would you best describe that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: He got -- he was in good relations with the Serbs. He worked in the water-supply company there, and he had many Serb acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what happened to Male Vishaj?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Male was also beaten by them. They removed his ring from his finger and returned the ring to him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described at page 8 of your statement - this is in the fourth paragraph - that you saw that the village was set on fire. Can you explain to us what it was that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: When the war started at around 9.00 they started to torch the houses, especially the most beautiful houses, those that were not finished completely, they were not that -- quite damaged; but the others were and they set fire to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I believe you also made some observations about seeing fires -- the setting of fires when you were being held in the room of the house. Is that accurate and can you explain what you saw then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The houses around the place where we were were all on fire, in flames.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you made those observations from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: In the house, the basement that was mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And so could you see out from the basement where you were to see those fires?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The basement was not finished completely. It was open upstairs, but later on we were taken outside by them, and you could clearly see that the whole village was burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving ahead a little bit, you explained at page 9 of your statement that in the morning a policeman came and told you to put women and children on tractors and to leave Beleg. Can you tell us how many people left that way?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That morning, the policeman came to the place where we were, he came to the second floor, and he said to us, Whoever has a tractor should collect the people and head towards Decan. There were many people there, children, women, and so on. On the 30th, they separated the youths and only the elderly, the women, and the children were allowed to get on the tractors and move towards Decan. They had to follow a field road that was going towards Gjakova and Decan. When we arrived at the tractors, there was police presence, there was -- there were Pinzgauers. When we arrived at Carrabreg, they told us to go back into the direction of Gjakova and proceed towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, perhaps you could explain that to us a little bit. Can you tell us who told you to go to Albania and how it was communicated?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The policemen; I don't know their names. We didn't know at that time that we were going to Albania. We were told initially that we were going to Decan, but when we arrived at Carrabreg, there we were told to go in the direction of Gjakove and from there towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I know you described escaping, and I'll have a question for you about that in a moment. But at the time that you were still with the group, could you make any observations about the police? Were they accompanying people as they went to Albania or how were the police positioned?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: When we arrived at Carrabreg, they told us to take the road towards Gjakova. The road was full of police and vehicles and Pinzgauers. The check-points that I passed through on the second location -- second occasion, because on the first occasion I got off and went to look for my family, that was in Beleg. I got off the tractor and Zekije Nitaj from my village started to drive the tractor in the direction of Albania. Myself I got off the tractor and through the fields I walked towards Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And you explained, I know, in your statement that after you escaped, you eventually made your way to Isniq. You then described the Serbs shelling Isniq. Can you tell us when it was that the Serbs shelled Isniq?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It's Isniq not Irzniq. I arrived in Isniq the following day. I remained there for two days. It's when the shelling started. There was so many people there. The whole village was filled with people. The fields around were filled with people. People from the villages of that municipality had all gathered there. The shelling was ongoing. Strellc was shelled and the villages around that area, they were shelling from the location called Podi i Geshtenjane then Suku i Biteshit and other positions occupied by the Serb police and military forces. Therefore, we were forced to leave this village too and head towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you are aware of any interactions with the police or police authorities in Isniq?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It was a huge crowd of people. The police in Decan issued the order to the police there that we had to leave that area, the chief of the police in the police station in Decan, Buda --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you just -- I think we had a problem with the interpretation - just repeat the last name. So the chief of the police at the police station in Decan and then we missed the last name --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Vukmir was his name known as Vula [Realtime transcript read in error, "Bula"] and his last name was Mircic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you just described in your last answer that the police in Decan issued the order that you had to leave, and then you mentioned something about the chief of police. Can you explain again for us what it was that the chief of police did?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I personally didn't talk to him, but the villagers from Isniq and the leaders in the village told us that we had to leave the village and head towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did the leaders of the village speak to the chief of police? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It was a huge crowd of people that we joined and people kept joining this convoy of people leaving Isniq towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Just to reiterate my question, maybe it's not coming through clearly. I'm just trying to understand your earlier answer, and I think there were some problems with the interpretation. Were there conversations with the chief of police that were communicated to you; and if so, can you explain those?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: When we joined the convoy, we were told that he had instructed some leaders, local policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: When you say "he," you mean the chief of police had instructed some leaders?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, Vula.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And what did he instruct them to do?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: He had instructed them to tell all the families there to leave the village and head towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that's clear. And can you tell us how you came to know that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Well, everybody left towards Albania. We joined that convoy. Everybody from every village in the municipality was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is really beyond 92 bis now, a completely new topic has been opened now which did not feature in the Milutinovic trial or in the statement. I did not want to interrupt earlier, but there were have been already questions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate the objection. I think I ended up spending a lot more time on that than I intended. I was just trying to clarify the answer. I don't have any more questions about that area, but I wanted to make sure that we had the answer clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, the final area of my questioning. You said that -- you say at the end of your statement that: "They took our documents and IDs in the Gjakova bridge called Ura e Shejte," [sic] I'm not sure if I'm pronouncing that right, it's S-h-e-j-t-e. Can I ask you, sir, who was it who took the documents from your group?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The documents and IDs were taken from us on the Ura e Shenjte bridge on the bridge in the direction of Gjakova. Whoever had money left on them, that money was also taken by the police that was positioned there near the Ura e Shenjte at Kodra e Shenjte; however, some documents were taken away from us the following day when we were at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, did they take documents from you particularly?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: They didn't take my documents. I removed them from my pockets because I knew they were going to take them away. I hid them in the tractor, in the hay in the tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did you see the police taking documents from others?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sure. I was just asking if you had seen the police taking documents from other people.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you explain who the other people were that you saw them taking documents from? You don't have to give the names, but were they the people that were with you? Were they farther away? If you could just tell that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: They took the documents from my father, mother, wife, and other co-villagers that were on the same tractor with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Those are my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mazrekaj. I'm Veljko Djurdjic --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- member of the Defence team for the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic, with the assistance of Ms. Marie O'Leary, also member of our team. I have a few questions for you. If a question is not clear to you, please let me know. I'll try to rephrase it. I'd like to start from your evidence given earlier today and some discrepancies I've noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for Exhibit P676 to be displayed on the screen, that's the transcript from the Milutinovic trial, page 5838, line 10 through 12. 5838, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have just said that at one of the bridges, documents were not taken away from you because you've -- you had hidden them, and here in the Milutinovic trial it says: "Q. ... did you turn over any documents that day? "A. No. I did not have any documents on me that day, so I didn't hand anything over."

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It is true that I said that. The reference was not made only to IDs or passports. It was a pile of documents, diplomas, certificates, that had taken -- been taken away at other check-points. The documents, these diplomas, certificates, these were the ones that I hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, is this quotation correct: "A. No. I did not have any documents on me, so I didn't hand anything over." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I did hear the readback of the transcript, and I heard that during the trial, that's why I mentioned at the outset that the interpretation was very bad during that trial. It was in B/C/S and I only wish that I had received interpretation in Albanian at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazrekaj. Let's move on. Earlier today, speaking of Istinic village, you said that the chief of SUP Decani gave an order and spoke to the population of Isniq village, saying that they had to go to Albania and you said they related this to you and you said a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we display page 5813 from the Milutinovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at lines 9 through 13. "A. I remember that day very well. I left the convoy and went to look for my relatives, my family. On the 30th, I arrived at Istinic and joined my family. On the 30th, shelling started, so we had to leave en masse, all the inhabitants that were in Isniq at the time ... had to go towards Albania." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: On the 30th - it's a mistake there - this is the first exit -- the first time when we left Beleg; the second time is in Isniq, not the 30th. We left Isniq two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I conclude that it was a misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Most probably. This is what I keep saying. I should have received interpretation in Albanian, not in B/C/S, so that I could explain things better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call up 5836, lines 7 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In response to the question: "Q. And now, when you went to Isniq to be with your family and then decided to leave for Albania, am I correct that at that point in time there were no policeman present who ordered you or otherwise told you to go to Albania, were there?" You answered: "A. There was a very large group of people in Isniq from different villages, and shelling started from Strellc, so from the western part of Isniq and from Podi i Geshtenjane. So the villagers said we had to leave and all of us took the way towards Albania." And then the question: "Q. And there were no policemen present at that time in the village when the villagers told you to leave and when you left for Albania?" Your answer: "A. I did not see them." Was this correctly interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: When the shelling started, it started from the direction of Podi i Geshtenjane. They shelled Strellc. The principal of the school, Nazif Ferizaj [phoen], was killed. The police was there on the road from Decan -- Peje-Decan road and the houses were being burned. That's why we had to leave Isniq and head towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, I read back to you this portion of the transcript. Now please tell me, was it correctly interpreted or not?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: In Serbian it was not correctly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just one last question relating to this. For the first time today you mentioned the chief of the SUP in Decani. You mentioned policemen and you did not mention any policemen or this conversation with the villagers, you didn't mention it in your -- in your testimony in Milutinovic nor in this 2004 statement. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It's known to everyone, Vula was the chief of the police for Decan community for 60.000 inhabitants. Vula was the one who, together with the police, drove us out of our homes, of our work. You know, they dismissed us. So he was the one who called on the Decane population to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mazrekaj, you are a teacher and you can understand my question well, so please answer my question. For the first time today you mentioned this chief of Decani police, this Vuleta Mircic, and for the first time, you've mentioned that the police told any of the villagers that they need to go to Albania and that this -- and that that was the reason why you headed for Albania. Why did you fail to mention that in the Milutinovic case when you testified here under oath and why was it missing from your 2004 statement? Please just explain that; if you cannot explain, we can just move on. There is no contest as to who was the chief of police in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: It is a fact that I didn't mention it because we had more dealings with the chiefs of the cross -- check-points, but everybody knew that he was leading the police who was number one among them. I have left out many things in my statement because what happened in Decan was a rare event in Kosova. I tried to include in it many things, but not everything because I really regret that many of them are not yet here in this Tribunal because we in our village have lost 171 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mazrekaj. You said today --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just need to explain something so that we can follow this more easily. The statement -- the 2002 statement, I marked paragraphs 1 through 65, and for each of these paragraph numbers I will mention the page in English and also in the Albanian version so that we can follow this more easily, and that's how I also prepared my notes here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2000 statement, the statement from 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've told us today - and this is in paragraph 61, in the English version this will be on page 10, and in Albanian it's also on page 10 - you've told us today that you were ordered to go to Djakovica and then on to Albania. And in your 2000 statement you say: "On the way to Decani I realised that we were being sent towards Djakovica, so I stopped to see my family." So you never said at any point there that anyone had ordered you to do so; this was your conclusion, rather.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I went to look for my family on the 30th. I left the convoy when we left Beleg. So it's not what you are putting to me, as what -- as you are saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you please read this portion: "On the way to Decani I realised that we were being directed towards Djakovica ..." Please read that portion if you can. You can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The road to Gjakove is the road to Albania. You have to change that. That is the direction towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We'll change that. Now, in paragraph 36 - in English that's page 11, the fifth paragraph from the top; and in the Albanian version that will be on page 6, the fourth paragraph from the top - Mr. Mazrekaj, - and I'm referring to this portion: "A group of villagers arrived and we went to discuss ..." So today for the first time you mention Arkan's and Seselj's men. Up until now I've noticed that there was no mention of them. You never mentioned them or described them. You did mention paramilitary units and you described what they were and this was in your testimony in the Milutinovic trial, but you never mentioned Seselj's and Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That's true because when we were in Beleg on the 29th and the 30th, we couldn't tell them from one another. But now and again I fainted because of being badly beaten. And I recall that they were situated in the children's resort house in Decan and then they came and surrounded Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you remembered to mention that today?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: [B/C/S interpretation] No, not today. I've said this before already. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right, we can move on. Now I would like to ask you when you went to Crnobreg for the first time to ask whether you may go to Isniq, could you just tell me, what was the village -- the name of the village that you said you were going to?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: [Albanian interpretation] Isniq, I went to Carrabreg to ask the police at the check-point to allow us to pass through the check-point and not be obliged to take the side-streets and walk through the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, so Isniq. Now please tell us who was in the car with you when you went to Crnobreg for the first time to ask whether you would be allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I was there two times. Are you asking me about the first or the second time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean the first time when you went there by car.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: During the first time was Zenel Zogaj [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask him to repeat the name of the person, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was no one else?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The second time there were other people, but I wasn't interested in them. We were in Zoran's car.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoran took our car, he confiscated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I only asked about the first time. Now let's move on. You've told us today - and this is in paragraph 23 of your statement, in English that's on page 4 and in Albanian it is also on page 4 - in this paragraph you say: "On the 27th March, 1999, around 8.30, I went out and saw the villagers who had gathered in the centre. Four families from the village of Sllup came to our village. Local Albanian policemen told us not to leave the village because nothing would happen to us." And today you told us that some policemen came and told you that because of bombing you had to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I think it's clear. The policemen who came to tell us to leave the village were from Decan police station. Those who told us to stay in the village were our co-villagers, local police. They thought that they were charged with a very noble function, to save us from the Serbs, but that was in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But in your statement you only mention four families from the Slup village --

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: [B/C/S interpretation] No, not four families but 37 people and it is clearly stated there. I have it in my brief-case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think here it is very clear in your statement. It says on the 27th of May -- March, but let's move on. We can see what's written there and the Trial Chamber will assess this. Mr. Mazrekaj, tell me, please, who did you stay with in Drenoc in 1999 or who did you live with in Drenoc in 1999, in March?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: [Albanian interpretation] You are asking me about my family or about the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about your family.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: With my wife, my mother, and my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, did you live in a joint household or were these separate families -- separate households?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: That's my house. I was born there, I was grown up there, it's not an alien house, it's my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I am right, you also had a brother. Did he live with you in the same house?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Even today we live together, but at the time he used to work in Peje. He is a well-known person, he is a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, your family property, the house that you had and the courtyard around it, was it fenced off with a wall?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: No, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which part was fenced off?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: Only the upper part, but there were no gates. The other part was fenced off with a wooden fence, then there were the stairs. Two times the police and the army settled in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How high was the fence, or rather, the wall?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: [B/C/S interpretation] Well, I didn't measure them. [Albanian interpretation] In some places 4 metres, in some places 2 metres. They destroyed the house and final they set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us on what material was the wall built on.

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The first floor was made of stone, the second floor was made of bricks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the wall, the wall around?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: In the upper part it was built of concrete blocks, on the western part with wood, on the southern part there was the haystack and it was also built with wooden planks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are familiar with the customs in the village in that area. Is it customary for the family properties to be walled-in, to be fenced-off with walls, such as the one that you had?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are asking me about. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In towns and also in villages in the area where you lived, in Decani and in other villages, in other parts of the country-side in Kosovo and Metohija, was it traditional to have walls around the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MEHMET MAZREKAJ
utterances.text: The one who can afford to can fence -- can build a fence around the house. There is not any custom that tells you to build a fence or not. Whoever can afford does that. It depends on the economic means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
